title: The acute effects of medium-chain triglyceride supplementation on metabolic rate and fat oxidation at rest in healthy young adults
abstract:
Introduction: Medium-chain triglycerides (MCT) are rapidly absorbed and metabolised for energy, yet evidence for their effects on resting metabolic rate (RMR) and fat oxidation in recreationally active young adults is limited and inconsistent. This study investigates the acute effects of MCT supplementation on RMR and fat oxidation at rest.

Methods: Nine healthy young adults (5 male, 4 female; aged 21.4±0.7 years; BMI 23.3±3.9 kg/m²) completed a before-and-after study. Breath-by-breath gas analysis measured RMR and substrate utilisation in a fasted, standardised state (no alcohol, caffeine or exercise the day prior). After baseline testing, participants consumed a drink containing 30 g MCT oil, 100 ml lactose-free low-fat milk and a teaspoon of cacao, returning after 3 hours for repeat testing.

Results: Acute MCT supplementation significantly reduced RER, indicating a shift towards fat oxidation at rest (pre 0.904 [0.876–0.933]; post 0.882 [0.863–0.894]; W=36.0, p=0.008). RMR did not change significantly (pre 2408 [1783–3181] kcal/day; post 2430 [1902–3239] kcal/day; W=15.0, p=0.742). Secondary outcomes were unchanged (p>0.05).

Conclusion: Acute ingestion of 30 g C8 MCT oil significantly reduced resting RER in young healthy adults, indicating greater fat oxidation, though RMR was largely unchanged. A larger sample with a control condition is needed to confirm these findings.

Key terms: medium-chain triglycerides; respiratory exchange ratio; resting metabolic rate; fat oxidation; indirect calorimetry.

title: The effects of Medium Chain Triglycerides on sports performance and energy expenditure in healthy young adults - A scoping review
abstract:
Background: Medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) have been proposed as a nutritional supplement to increase sports performance and metabolic output by increasing fat oxidation. However, the existing literature is limited and the findings are often conflicting. This scoping review maps the available evidence on MCT supplementation and exercise performance and metabolism in healthy young adults.

Method: A scoping review was carried out following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, searching PubMed, ScienceDirect and Embase. Studies were included if they involved young healthy participants, MCT supplementation and outcomes relating to exercise performance and metabolism (both acute and chronic supplementation regimes). Data were extracted using a template built in Covidence.

Results: From 1093 studies, 16 met the inclusion criteria after screening — most were cross-over trials in trained or healthy adults. MCT supplementation increased ketone production and fatty-acid oxidation, but effects on exercise performance were mixed: high acute doses decreased performance due to gastrointestinal discomfort, while chronic supplementation showed some evidence of improved endurance and energy output. Evidence for increased energy expenditure and carbohydrate sparing was inconsistent.

Discussion: The conflicting results likely reflect the heterogeneity of the included studies (design, participant characteristics, dose and timing). While there may be changes in substrate utilisation, these do not necessarily translate to improved performance.

Conclusion: MCT increases fat oxidation during exercise, but physical performance effects are inconsistent. Further research is needed on optimal dosing and long-term effects.

Keywords: medium-chain triglycerides; exercise performance; fat oxidation; metabolism.
